newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss say no evidence coins had Holocaust gold.
newsitem.headline: Swiss say no evidence coins had Holocaust gold.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank said on Thursday it had no evidence that coins it minted after World War Two were made with gold stolen from Holocaust victims.

Replying to questions about allegations made in a British television documentary, central bank vice-chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said SNB tests found no indication that those minted after the war might have come from gold remelted from victims' teeth.

The BBC television report this week had said tests by a California university on post-war Swiss gold coins found high levels of mercury, which the report said suggested the metal came from dental gold.
But Roth told a news conference the bank's own tests of coins from 1907 through 1949 found higher mercury levels only in the series from 1913 and 1927.
"We have no evidence in Switzerland (to support the BBC claims)," Roth told reporters.
"Mercury is used in the first stage of refining gold, in the mines, to separate gold from other metals, so it is no surprise there are traces of mercury in gold," Roth said.
The SNB has acknowledged since the 1980s that gold it bought during the war from Hitler's Reichsbank may have been looted by Nazi Germany.
But Roth said all coins minted in 1945 and 1946 were made from gold stocks that the bank knew pre-dated World war Two.
This decision was made by the SNB because Switzerland was in post-war talks with the Allies about demands for the return of gold stolen by Nazi Germany from occupied countries.
Under the 1946 Washington Accord, Berne gave the Allies 250 million Swiss francs worth of gold in return for the Western powers' dropping any further claims to SNB gold stocks.

Roth also said the 1945 and 1946 coins were backdated to 1935. But he said the backdating was done because of a technicality, not to hide their time of origin, and the coins were specially marked as "35L".

The reason for the backdating was a revaluation of the Swiss franc in 1936, Roth said. Because the franc was a gold-backed currency, the revaluation changed the amount of gold that should go into a franc-denominated coin.
The backdating stopped with another change in the law in 1946 and coins from 1947 on carried the actual date, he said.
